Case Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 63-year-old married man of Oceania descent, who works as the publisher of a small, independent press. He presents as a dignified, articulate man, though his hands tremble slightly as he adjusts his glasses. He has been married for thirty-eight years to his wife, Leilani, who he describes as his "anchor." Over several sessions, a coherent narrative of his suffering has emerged.

The event that broke his world occurred two years ago, during a regional book fair on a neighboring island. A fire, later determined to be arson, swept through the convention center’s main hall. Mr. A. had been on a mezzanine level, negotiating a distribution deal. He remembers the precise, acrid smell of melting plastic before the alarms sounded. He remembers the crush of bodies, the frantic shouts, and the impossible, suffocating heat. He guided a group of authors toward a fire exit, his mind working on pure instinct. In the chaos, he saw a young woman, an intern from a rival publisher, trip and fall. He went back for her. He pulled her to her feet, but a falling beam of burning timber separated them. He does not know if she made it out. He never learned her name.

In the present, Mr. A. cannot walk into a large indoor space without his heart hammering against his ribs. The small, cramped office of his publishing house has become a sanctuary, but also a cage. He holds editorial meetings in the hallway, claiming the conference room is "too stuffy." He has stopped attending book fairs or literary festivals entirely, delegating the task to his junior editors. He tells himself it is a matter of "changing priorities," but he knows the truth: the thought of a crowded exhibition hall, the smell of fresh paper and coffee, triggers a visceral, blinding panic.

His sleep is a battleground. He wakes three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, the phantom smell of smoke in his nostrils. In his dreams, he is always running, but his legs are heavy, like they are made of stone. He sees the young woman’s face, not her features, but the shape of her terror. He has learned to stay up late, reading manuscripts until his eyes burn, to minimize the time spent in the dark. Leilani finds him at 3 a.m., staring at a blank wall, a cup of cold tea untouched beside him.

At work, his memory is failing him. He, who once knew the page count and ISBN of every book on his list, now forgets author names and misses deadlines. He has become irrationally irritable with his staff, snapping at an assistant for a misplaced comma, then retreating into a cold silence of guilt. He has begun to insist on a strict "no candles" policy in the office, and he flinches when the office coffee machine hisses steam. He avoids the fire escape stairwell, taking the elevator even to go down one floor, his hands shaking as he presses the button.

He describes a "deadness" that has settled over him. The passion he once felt for a beautifully crafted sentence, for a debut novel, for the act of bringing a story into the world, is gone. He feels like a fraud, going through the motions. He pushes his food around his plate at dinner, losing fifteen pounds in six months. He tells Leilani he is "fine," but he has stopped reaching for her hand. The greatest intimacy he can now manage is a shared silence, a silence that feels less like peace and more like a shared, unspoken grief for the man he used to be. He does not speak of the fire. He cannot. The story is trapped inside him, a splinter of hot metal he cannot remove. He is a publisher without a story, a man drowning in the wake of a single, terrible moment.
